A quarrel broke out between my chauffeur and the gardener. How should I handle the matter?
Speak with each separately to understand the trouble, then settle the matter quietly and fairly without embarrassing either man.
My sister-in-law and I disagreed sharply over the seating at a family christening. What should I do now?
Discuss the seating calmly beforehand, and if disagreement remains, yield gracefully rather than let the christening be marred by dispute.
Two old friends of mine quarreled at my card party and now refuse to speak. What is my role as hostess?
Arrange the tables so each may enjoy the evening without forced proximity, hoping time and kindness will mend what was broken.
My husband quarreled with our host over business before dinner. How ought I to behave at the table?
Behave with unruffled graciousness toward our host, letting no trace of the private quarrel disturb the pleasantness of the evening.
My niece and her fiancé had a public quarrel at the engagement luncheon. How should I, as her aunt, respond?
Draw attention away from the disagreement with a graceful remark, allowing the young couple privacy to settle their differences later.
A quarrel has arisen between two of my bridesmaids over their dresses. How shall I resolve it before the wedding?
Speak with each privately, hear their concerns with patience, and find a solution that leaves both feeling valued and at ease before the wedding.
A guest has overstayed her welcome by several days. How might I encourage her departure?
You may gently mention an upcoming engagement that requires the room, allowing her to depart with her dignity intact and no unpleasantness between you.
My cousin's manners are rough, yet she is coming to stay. How do I make her feel welcome?
Greet her as warmly as any other guest and quietly guide her, in private, on any small point of custom, so she never feels singled out.
What is proper when an unexpected caller arrives just as we are sitting down to dine?
Invite the caller warmly to join you, and if the table cannot accommodate another, arrange a light refreshment served with equal courtesy.
How ought I to treat a guest whose family is of lesser standing than my own?
Receive her with the same warmth you would show any guest, for true hospitality does not weigh the standing of those it welcomes.
A visitor has arrived without notice at an inconvenient hour. What is the proper response?
Receive the visitor pleasantly regardless of the hour, and if the moment is truly inconvenient, say so kindly and propose a better time.
How should I handle a guest who brings along an uninvited companion?
Welcome the companion as cordially as the guest herself, for graciousness extended to the unexpected reflects best upon the household.
What should be done if a guest arrives while the house is not yet properly tidied?
Receive the guest with unhurried composure, apologizing lightly if needed, and never allow household disorder to trouble her comfort.
How does one manage a guest who has clearly overindulged at dinner?
Say nothing of it at all, and see that she is quietly and kindly assisted to rest, sparing her any embarrassment.
What is the correct way to greet visitors who call at an unfashionable hour merely to see the new furnishings?
Receive them cheerfully and take genuine pleasure in showing your home, for curiosity kindly indulged makes friends of casual callers.
How should a hostess behave when a guest declines nearly every dish offered?
Offer once with warmth and let the matter rest, ensuring she is never made to feel conspicuous for her preferences.
What ought I to do when a guest arrives in clothing plainly unsuited to the occasion?
Say nothing whatsoever of her dress, and greet her exactly as warmly as you would any other guest properly attired.
How should I receive a guest who has come merely out of social obligation and not true friendship?
Offer her the same genuine warmth you would any welcome guest, for true hospitality does not depend upon the visitor's motive.
What is proper when a visitor's child misbehaves during a call?
Overlook the small disturbance with good humor, perhaps offering a toy or biscuit, so mother and child both feel at ease.
How does one manage guests of very differing ages at the same gathering?
See that conversation and comfort are extended equally to young and old alike, so that no guest feels overlooked.
What should be done if a caller arrives while I am occupied with private correspondence?
Set your correspondence aside promptly and greet her without delay, for a visitor's time deserves as much respect as one's own.
How ought a hostess act when two guests who dislike one another must be entertained together?
Arrange the seating and conversation thoughtfully so that both may pass the evening pleasantly and without unnecessary friction.
What is correct when a guest praises a dish that was, in truth, poorly made?
Thank her simply and warmly, and think no more of the matter, for a guest's kindness deserves nothing but gracious acceptance.
How should one behave toward a visitor who has clearly come uninvited to view the house out of curiosity alone?
Show her the house as courteously as any true guest, for hospitality is not diminished by a visitor's motive.
What is proper when a guest arrives bearing a gift that is plainly unsuitable or of poor quality?
Receive it with sincere gratitude and give it a place of honor for the duration of her visit, whatever its merit.
How does one handle a servant's small error while guests are present in the parlor?
Overlook the small error before the guests entirely, and speak to her kindly and privately afterward if correction is needed.
My houseguest sleeps until noon each day. How ought I to manage this?
Simply have a cold breakfast kept ready under a cloth for whenever she rises, and say nothing of the hour; a guest's rest is her own affair while she is under your roof.
How should I seat a guest who is known to snore terribly, so as not to embarrass him?
Give him a room at the quiet end of the house, away from other sleepers, and mention nothing of the matter to him or to anyone else.
My children's nurse asks for an hour's rest in the afternoon. Ought I to grant it?
Certainly; a tired nurse is no comfort to a child, and an hour's quiet in the afternoon will serve the whole household better than any scolding.
A guest dozed off during my dinner party. How shall I handle it gracefully?
Speak softly to rouse him with some small pleasant remark, as though nothing at all were amiss, and steer the talk elsewhere at once.
Is it proper to wake a sleeping guest for a scheduled outing?
Knock softly and speak his name gently; give him a few moments before he must appear, so he need not feel hurried or ashamed.
What is the correct way to arrange sleeping quarters when I have more guests than beds?
Offer the best room to the eldest or least hardy among your guests, and see that every arrangement, however modest, is made comfortable and explained kindly beforehand.
My guest wishes to retire earlier than the rest of the party. How should I respond?
Wish her a pleasant good night at once and see her comfortably to her room, so the others may continue without the smallest awkwardness.
Should I wake my servants earlier than usual when guests are expected?
Give them fair notice the evening before, so they may rise in good time without being startled or overworked for the sake of a single morning.
My aunt insists on an afternoon nap even when we have callers. How should I explain her absence?
Say simply that she is resting and will join them presently; there is no shame in a nap, and none need be implied.
A guest overslept and missed the appointed breakfast hour entirely. What is the proper response?
Have something kept warm for him and greet him as pleasantly as if he had arrived on the very stroke of the hour.
How do I politely handle a guest who naps with her door wide open and speaks in her sleep?
Close the door gently as you pass, and never mention the matter to her or to anyone else.
My husband dozes off in church some Sundays. How should I manage this without shame?
Touch his sleeve gently and rest a hand on his arm; a quiet gesture spares him embarrassment far better than any public remark.
Is it rude for a guest to ask for a rest before dinner after a long journey?
Not in the least; show him to his room at once and delay dinner a little if you can, for a weary guest deserves consideration before ceremony.
What should I do if my maid falls asleep while sitting up for the family's late return?
Wake her gently and thank her for waiting; better still, tell her beforehand not to sit up so late on your account.
How ought I to speak of a friend who is known to require a great deal of sleep?
Say only that she keeps to her own hours, as every person is entitled to do, and let the subject drop there.
My guest wishes to rest quietly in the afternoon while the rest of us wish to play cards. What is proper?
Move the card table to another room and see that her door is not disturbed; her comfort need not spoil anyone's pleasure.
Should I rouse a sickly relative from her rest merely because callers have arrived?
No; explain to the callers that she is resting on the doctor's advice, and let her sleep undisturbed.
Is it acceptable to tease a guest who slept through breakfast, lunch, and nearly dinner?
It is far kinder to say nothing at all, and simply see that a good meal awaits him whenever he does appear.
How should I arrange the household when an elderly guest requires far more rest than the rest of us?
Quiet the household somewhat during her resting hours and see that meals may be brought to her whenever she requires them.
What is the proper way to handle two guests sharing a room when one keeps far later hours than the other?
Mention the difference in habits to each beforehand, so they may agree quietly between themselves how best to manage the room.
What is the proper way to receive guests when a sudden rainstorm ruins their arrival?
Welcome them warmly, offer dry wraps and a seat by the fire, and make no mention of their bedraggled appearance so they may feel at ease at once.
How ought one to plan a garden party if the forecast threatens rain?
Arrange a modest indoor alternative in advance, so that no guest need suffer the weather's caprice on your account.
What should a hostess do when winter's early dark forces guests to leave before dessert is served?
Serve refreshments promptly, mindful of the shortened afternoon, so every guest may enjoy the full visit before nightfall.
Is it proper to comment on a guest's heavy winter coat upon their arrival?
Offer to hang it in a warm closet and say nothing of its wear, for comfort in the cold is a kindness, not a fashion trial.
How does one behave toward a servant who is late fetching firewood on a frigid morning?
Thank him warmly once the wood arrives, remembering that ice and snow slow even the most willing hands.
What is proper etiquette for a summer picnic when the heat proves unbearable to some guests?
Move the gathering promptly to shade or indoors, ensuring the comfort of all before continuing the festivities.
Should one apologize for a chilly parlor when guests arrive in the depths of winter?
Simply apologize briefly and see that the fire is stoked at once, sparing the guests any further discomfort.
How should a hostess handle an autumn tea when leaves and mud are tracked indoors?
Have a mat and cloth ready near the door and mention the mud lightly, if at all, so no guest feels embarrassed.
What is correct when a snowstorm forces overnight guests to stay unexpectedly?
Offer them the warmest guest room available and extra blankets, treating the inconvenience as no burden at all.
How does one greet friends who arrive late to a spring luncheon due to unpredictable showers?
Greet them warmly and quietly have a plate kept ready, understanding that weather is beyond anyone's control.
What should be done if a summer heatwave spoils the ices before the party begins?
Explain simply that the heat has affected the sweets, and offer a cool substitute with good cheer.
Is it proper to complain of the cold in front of one's guests during a winter visit?
Bear the chill graciously and quietly ask that the fire be built higher, without burdening guests with complaint.
How should one handle guests who track slush indoors during a February visit?
Have the floor cleaned discreetly afterward, and think no more of it, for slush is the season's common trial.
What is correct behavior when a summer thunderstorm frightens a nervous guest?
Draw the curtains, light a lamp, and speak of pleasant matters until the storm has passed and calm is restored.
How should a host respond when unseasonable cold forces cancellation of an outdoor wedding?
Arrange an indoor alternative swiftly and reassure the anxious couple that all will yet be lovely.
What is the proper way to receive callers who arrive soaked from an unexpected spring shower?
Offer towels and dry seating at once, saying only that such showers are the season's small mischief.
How ought one address the discomfort of guests during an unusually hot autumn afternoon?
Adjust the menu to lighter, cooling fare, showing consideration for the guests' comfort in the unexpected warmth.
What should be done if frost ruins the flowers meant for a winter dinner table?
Substitute simple greenery or candles with grace, and think nothing more of the frost's small theft.
How does one behave when a sudden gale disrupts an outdoor autumn gathering?
Usher everyone indoors promptly and calmly, making the shift seem no trouble at all.
Is it proper to mention how cold a guest's hands are upon greeting them in deep winter?
Offer a warm cup of tea and a seat near the fire without remark, letting warmth speak for itself.
A rival has spread an unflattering rumour about my family. How do I restore our good name?
Bear yourself with quiet dignity and let your conduct, rather than counter-accusation, speak for your character; time and good behaviour are the surest restoratives of a tarnished name.
How ought I respond when someone questions my honour at a dinner party?
Answer calmly and without heat, for a composed reply defends one's honour far better than an angry retort, and preserves the harmony of the table besides.
My brother's gambling debts threaten our family's reputation. What is the correct social response?
Address the matter privately and with compassion, offering what steady counsel you can, for family honour is best preserved by loyalty shown quietly rather than by public disavowal.
Is it proper to correct a guest who has misrepresented my late husband's character?
A gentle, private word setting the record straight is far more fitting than a public correction, which would embarrass both your guest and yourself.
How should I handle a social slight that questions my integrity?
Meet the slight with unruffled courtesy; a person of true integrity need not stoop to retaliation to prove the fact.
What is the proper way to defend one's honour when falsely accused at a social gathering?
State the truth plainly and without agitation, trusting that honesty delivered with composure will persuade reasonable company far better than indignation.
My cousin's scandalous engagement threatens the family name. How should I conduct myself in society?
Continue to treat your cousin with warmth and discretion in public, for loyalty in adversity does far more credit to a family's name than any distancing gesture.
How do I respond gracefully when my honesty is doubted by an acquaintance?
Respond with patience and a clear account of the facts; a reputation for honesty is best defended by continuing to act honestly, not by casting doubt upon another.
Is it acceptable to defend my honour by exposing a friend's indiscretion in return?
No; true honour is defended by one's own steady conduct, not by dragging another's failings into the light merely to even a score.
What should I do if my good name is questioned because of my husband's business failure?
Carry yourself with the same warmth and dignity as before, for a wife's character need not rise or fall with the fortunes of business, and true friends will understand this.
How ought one to behave when a rival tries to damage one's reputation before mutual friends?
Behave with unwavering courtesy toward all present, and allow your consistent good conduct over time to answer the rival's insinuations far more convincingly than words could.
My family name has been dishonoured by a distant relative's scandal. What is the proper social response?
Acknowledge the connection honestly if asked, and let your own conduct demonstrate that one relative's misstep does not define the character of the whole family.
How should I respond to a whispered insult about my honour overheard at a party?
It is best to let the insult pass unremarked in the moment, addressing it privately and calmly with the person later, so that dignity is preserved on both sides.
Is it proper to publicly shame someone who has slandered my reputation?
No; a private and composed conversation, seeking correction rather than humiliation, is the more honourable course and reflects better upon your own character.
How do I maintain my honour when a servant's error is mistaken for my own poor judgment?
Quietly clarify the matter without assigning blame in company, and address the error with the servant privately and kindly afterward.
What is the correct way to respond when one's word of honour is doubted at a business dinner?
Reaffirm your word with quiet confidence and let subsequent conduct prove its worth, for consistency of character is the best answer to doubt.
How should I behave toward a friend who unwittingly damaged my honour with a careless remark?
Accept the apology graciously and put the matter behind you, for a true friend's carelessness is more easily forgiven than remembered.
Is it proper to remind guests of a past favour when my honour in a matter is questioned?
It is better to let past kindnesses go unmentioned and to address the present doubt on its own honest terms.
How does one preserve one's honour when a social equal spreads false stories about one's conduct?
Preserve it through calm, truthful correction wherever necessary, and by continuing to act in a manner that leaves the false stories unconvincing to sensible company.
What is the proper etiquette for defending a family member's honour without causing a public scene?
Defend them firmly but quietly, choosing a private moment or a measured word rather than a public display, so that loyalty and decorum are both well served.
My aunt left me the family silver, but my cousin covets it. How ought I to inform her of the bequest?
Tell her privately and with warmth, assuring her that her own affection for your aunt was never in question, and offer to share some small keepsake so she need not feel forgotten.
How should I address my brother, who feels slighted by our father's will?
Speak with him face to face, listen fully to his grievance, and be willing to discuss whether some fairer division might ease his heart, even if the law already favors you.
What is the proper way to announce a large inheritance to relatives who received nothing?
Tell them quietly and privately, before any public gathering, so they may absorb the news with dignity and not be made to perform composure before others.
My grandmother's house has passed to me alone. How do I tell my siblings without unpleasantness?
Explain the matter honestly and kindly, and propose that they remain welcome in the house whenever they wish, so the property does not become a wall between you.
Ought I to correct a relative who exaggerates their claim to a family estate at dinner parties?
Draw them aside quietly afterward and gently clarify the facts, sparing them the embarrassment of a public correction.
How should I behave toward a cousin who contests my late uncle's will?
Treat her with patience and courtesy throughout, and encourage your solicitor to settle matters as swiftly and fairly as the law allows.
What is the correct etiquette for dividing my mother's jewelry among my sisters?
Lay every piece upon the table together and let each sister choose in turn, taking care that sentiment, not merely value, guides the division.
How ought I respond when a nephew hints broadly that he expects to inherit my country house?
Tell him plainly and kindly what your intentions are, so that he need not live in false hope nor unnecessary anxiety.
My husband's family disputes my right to his property. How should I conduct myself at family gatherings now?
Remain composed and civil, addressing the dispute honestly when asked, and take care that your grief for him is not overshadowed by the quarrel.
What is proper when a servant of many years is left a small legacy by my father, and my siblings object?
Defend the legacy firmly to your siblings, reminding them of her long and faithful service, and see that it is paid to her promptly and without diminishment.
How do I tell my late husband's children that the estate passes to my own children instead?
Tell them yourself, gently and in person, acknowledging their attachment to their father's home even as you explain the arrangement.
My sister insists I owe her a share of the farm though the will names me alone. How should I respond?
Hear her reasoning fully and honestly consider whether some equitable arrangement might be made, even beyond what the will strictly requires.
What is proper conduct when reading a will aloud to assembled relatives?
Read the document plainly and without embellishment, and afterward offer a kind word to any who seem troubled by its contents.
How should I handle a relative who forges affection only after learning of an inheritance?
Receive her kindly as always, but let your decisions be guided by long acquaintance and true regard rather than any sudden show of warmth.
What is the proper way to discuss my will with my children while I am still living?
Speak with them openly and together, if possible, so that your intentions are understood clearly and no one is left to guess or suspect.
My late father's second wife claims a share of property he promised to me. How should I proceed?
Approach the matter through proper legal counsel, treating her with civility throughout, whatever the outcome of the claim may be.
How do I tell a poor relation that the family estate will not extend to supporting her further?
Explain the situation kindly and clearly, and if any small assistance can still be offered, extend it with warmth rather than obligation.
What is proper when my brother assumes he will inherit the family business, but our father intends otherwise?
Encourage our father to speak with him honestly and soon, so he may adjust his expectations with dignity rather than shock.
How should I behave toward a cousin who was left out of my grandfather's will entirely?
Treat her exactly as you always have, with warmth and inclusion, so she is not made to feel the omission any more keenly than necessary.
What is correct when dividing family land between myself and a half-sibling I barely know?
Approach the division fairly and openly, taking the opportunity to know her better rather than letting the property stand between you.
How ought I treat the porter who brings my trunks to the platform?
One thanks the porter warmly and tips him fairly for his trouble, remembering that a kind word costs nothing and is long remembered.
What is the correct way to secure the best seat in a railway carriage?
Take your own seat promptly and courteously, but never claim more room than you require, so that fellow travellers may be seated in comfort.
My compartment companion is a chatty stranger. How should I discourage her?
Answer her pleasantly for a little while, then gently excuse yourself with your book or your view, so that she is not made to feel unwelcome.
How does one behave when a fellow passenger's child is restless on a long journey?
One overlooks a little childish restlessness with patience, perhaps offering the mother a kind word, for a long journey tries the youngest travellers most.
What should I say to the conductor who has made an honest error with my ticket?
One points out the error quietly and courteously, allowing the conductor to correct it without embarrassment, for such mistakes happen to the best of us.
How should I greet friends who have come to see me off at the station?
One greets them with real warmth and gratitude for their kindness in coming, and lingers a moment to bid them a proper farewell.
What is proper when I wish to change compartments to avoid an unpleasant travelling companion?
One may ask the guard quietly for another seat, without drawing attention to the other passenger or causing them needless embarrassment.
How does a lady behave toward a gentleman who offers to lift her bag onto the rack?
One accepts such kindness with a gracious thank-you, for it costs nothing to acknowledge a small courtesy sincerely offered.
What should be done if the dining car is crowded and I must share a table with strangers?
One shares the table amiably, offering a friendly word or two, for good company often makes a railway meal quite pleasant.
How should I address the sleeping-car attendant who wakes me too early?
One may mention the matter gently at a better hour, for the attendant means only to be helpful and deserves a courteous reminder, not a scolding.
What is correct when a fellow traveller asks to borrow my newspaper?
One lends it readily and pleasantly, for such small favours cost nothing and make a shared journey more agreeable for all.
How ought I behave toward the station master when my train is delayed?
One inquires patiently after the cause and expected delay, remembering the station master is rarely to blame and deserves civility even amid inconvenience.
What should I do if I notice a fellow passenger has left something behind at the last stop?
One informs the guard at once, so that word may be sent ahead and the article restored to its rightful owner without delay.
How should I treat a travelling companion of a lower station than my own?
One treats every travelling companion with equal courtesy, for good manners recognise no difference of station within a shared carriage.
What is proper conduct when boarding ahead of others at a crowded platform?
One waits one's turn and assists those slower or more burdened, for a little patience at the platform spares everyone a great deal of jostling.
How should I respond if the ticket inspector questions my ticket in front of others?
One answers calmly and produces the ticket promptly, sparing both oneself and the inspector any unnecessary unpleasantness before the other passengers.
What ought I say to a fellow traveller who admires my luggage rather too openly?
One accepts the compliment simply and turns the conversation kindly, perhaps admiring something of hers in return.
How should one behave toward the tea-trolley attendant who moves slowly through the carriage?
One waits with patience and thanks the attendant kindly when he arrives, for he has likely many carriages yet to serve.
What is correct when an elderly passenger struggles to find her seat?
One rises at once to assist her to her seat, offering a kind word, for such small helpfulness is the truest mark of good breeding.
How should I part from acquaintances met only during the journey once the train arrives?
One bids them a warm and pleasant farewell, thanking them for their company, for even a brief friendship deserves a gracious close.
